sources.citation: New Tribes Mission. 1992. [Genesis 1-3: 'Sabata 1', 'Sabata 2', 'Sabata 3'.] Goroka: New Tribes Mission-Publications (imprint '1992/165'). 8 pp. scan. Catalogued by The Rosetta Project / OLAC as 'Amto Genesis Translation' (archive.org rosettaproject_amt_gen-1); find.bible 'Bible Portions in Amto (1992)'.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing: vernacular scripture text in a plain roman practical orthography (scanned renders two special vowel letters as 'c' and 'T'), no diacritics, no stress or tone marks, no orthography or pronunciation note. Its value for amt is negative evidence (the only 'Amto' vernacular publication on record is actually Siawi) and a pointer that NTM/Ethnos360 holds the unpublished Siawi phonemic write-up, not an Amto one.

sources.citation: Steer, Martin. 2005. Languages of the Upper Sepik and Central New Guinea. Report prepared for the Upper Sepik-Central New Guinea Project (USCNGP); edits and Appendix 9.2 by Barry Craig, 2011. 60 pp. Section 2 'Amto-Musian Family: Amto', pp. 10-11.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology content for Amto: location, population, classification history (Loving & Bass 1964 Busa phylum vs Conrad & Dye 1975 29% with Musian), 4-10% lexical resemblance with Arai attributed to borrowing. Phonology sections in the report exist only for Mountain Ok (sec. 7.4).

sources.citation: Craig, Barry. 1980. Legends of the Amto, Simaiya Valley (including a brief description of the material culture). Oral History 8(4): 59-113 [Glottolog ref 300380 gives pp. 1-113]; revised web edition 'Legends of the Amto of Simaiya Valley, West Sepik Province, PNG', USCNGP, 56 pp; with companion 'Introduction to the Legends of the Abau of Idam Valley and of the Amto of Simaiya Valley' (orig. Oral History 8(4): 1-44), rev. web ed. 33 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No phonology content: 16 myths in English translation with occasional Amto words (e.g. fokiya 'dance house', arrow type waipa, tree names) in plain roman spelling without stress or tone marks; the Introduction has only a classification paragraph after Loving & Bass 1964 and mentions CMML linguist David Bailey at Green River.

sources.citation: Conrad, Robert J. & T. Wayne Dye. 1975. Some language relationships in the Upper Sepik region of Papua New Guinea. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 18 (Pacific Linguistics A-40), 1-35. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-A40.1.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 3.2 Amto-Musan Family (pp. 19-20): speakers, villages, 29% cognates, sound correspondences (Amto u, o/a, k, p, n/r, h ~ Musan); no Amto phonology. The paper's only stress remark ('Contrastive word stress was noted in Ama, and possibly in Rocky Peak, Bo, and Owiniga', Figure C) is about the Arai/Left May family, not Amto. Amto otherwise appears only as a column in the comparative wordlists.

sources.citation: Laycock, D. C. 1975. Isolates: Sepik Region. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study, vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene (Pacific Linguistics C-38), 879-886. Canberra: ANU.

sources.note: Sec. 2.15.1.2.4 AMTO (Ki), pp. 883-884: classification history only (Loving & Bass 1964 'Busa Phylum' rejected; 29% probable cognates with Musian per Conrad & Dye 1975; Bailey's wordlists); ends 'No data is available on typological features.' Nothing on stress.
